rule_summary: There is no absolute age limit for foster carers. Bufdir says that ideally you should be between 25 and 67.
notes: Humana says people under 25 are approved only as an exception. Tønsberg kommune asks for an age between 25 and 60.

rule_summary: Only people aged 25 or over can adopt or get prior consent to adopt. Someone aged 20 or over can still adopt if they and the child are already closely attached.
notes: Read in the act as passed by the Storting (Lovvedtak 104 (2016–2017)). Lovdata, which holds the current consolidated text, does not allow automated reading (robots.txt). A person without legal capacity in personal matters can adopt only if already closely attached to the child and the guardian agrees.

rule_summary: Bufdir gives 67 as the ideal upper age for foster carers, but sets no absolute limit.
notes: Humana says Bufetat uses an upper limit of 67 and that emergency carers can be older.

rule_summary: Tønsberg kommune says foster carers should be between 25 and 60.
notes: A municipal page, not a national rule.

rule_summary: There is no upper age in the law or the regulations. As a guide, the age gap between applicants and the child should be no more than 45 years when prior consent is given.
notes: Bufdir's adoption circular, last revised June 2026, read on bufdir.no. Applicants must be able to care for the child until adulthood. A large age gap between the two applicants also counts.

rule_summary: Married couples, cohabitants, single people and same-sex partners can foster. Couples should have a stable relationship and ideally have lived together for at least 2 years.
notes: Someone who is separated or divorced must have settled the emotional, legal and financial side. Single carers need a strong support network.

rule_summary: Only spouses and cohabitants can adopt together. Cohabitants means two people who live together in a stable, marriage-like relationship, and someone in a couple can usually only adopt with their partner.
notes: Read in the act as passed by the Storting (Lovvedtak 104 (2016–2017)). Lovdata, which holds the current consolidated text, does not allow automated reading (robots.txt). Exceptions cover a partner who has disappeared or has a serious mental illness or intellectual disability, and adopting a partner's child, one's own child or a former adoptive child.

rule_summary: Single people can adopt if they can take sole care of a child. Only applicants who live alone count as single.
notes: Read in the act as passed by the Storting (Lovvedtak 104 (2016–2017)). Lovdata, which holds the current consolidated text, does not allow automated reading (robots.txt). Bufdir's circular asks single applicants to have a stable network of family and friends.

rule_summary: For adoption from abroad, spouses or cohabitants must as a rule have lived together for the last 2 years before they apply.
legal_citation: Forskrift om adopsjon (FOR-2018-06-22-959) § 1; Bufdir Rundskriv 2020-08 (adoption casework), section 8.6.1
notes: Bufdir's adoption circular, last revised June 2026, read on bufdir.no. The regulations allow exceptions, for example where the couple have children together or have bought a home together.

rule_summary: Foster carers come from many cultures and backgrounds. Bufdir says more carers with a multicultural background who speak different languages are needed.
Couples of the same sex or of different sexes can apply to adopt.
notes: Colombia, the only country of origin at present, may set other requirements.

rule_summary: Your Norwegian must be good enough to look after the child in dealings with school and the wider community.

There is no income requirement beyond a safe and stable economy, with income and spending in balance over time. People who are unemployed or on disability or work assessment benefits can foster if their finances are in order.
Applicants must have a stable family economy, with income, spending, assets and debt in balance.
legal_citation: Forskrift om adopsjon (FOR-2018-06-22-959) § 1; Bufdir Rundskriv 2020-08 (adoption casework), section 8.6.3
notes: Bufdir's adoption circular, last revised June 2026, read on bufdir.no.

rule_summary: Usually one foster parent is released from ordinary work (frikjøp) when the child moves in, with pay for lost income agreed with the municipality. Many return to work after the first period.
notes: The basic allowance is paid whether or not a carer is released from work.

rule_summary: Bufdir recommends a standard first release period set by the child's age on moving in: 56 weeks for ages 0 to 1, 46 weeks for 2 to 5, 42 weeks for 6 to 12 and 22 weeks for 13 to 18.
notes: Bufdir's professional recommendations on financial terms for foster homes. Lost income is covered up to a guide ceiling of 6 G. A criteria model helps municipalities decide on release beyond the first period.

rule_summary: Foster parents in paid work have a right to 2 weeks' care leave when they take over care of a child under 15. In most cases they also have parents' rights to sick-child days, unpaid leave and shorter hours.
notes: Unpaid parental leave can be up to three years in total if the child is under 15.

rule_summary: Physical and mental health must be good enough to care for children with high needs. A health certificate from the GP, and any specialists, is gathered during the process. Disability or a chronic illness need not rule you out.
notes: Bufdir also asks for moderate alcohol use. It publishes a health certificate form (helseattest) for the GP to fill in.

rule_summary: Applicants send a health self-declaration and a doctor's statement. Bufetat judges whether any illness or disability affects care now and in future. As a rule, consent to adopt from abroad is not given to people who need daily medicine for serious mental illness to function.
legal_citation: Forskrift om adopsjon (FOR-2018-06-22-959) § 1; Bufdir Rundskriv 2020-08 (adoption casework), section 8.6.3
notes: Bufdir's adoption circular, last revised June 2026, read on bufdir.no. The document list is on Bufdir's page on adopting through an organisation.

rule_summary: There should be no smoking indoors in the home.
Your housing should be stable: you own the home or rent it on a long-term lease, with no plans to move soon. If you moved recently, you should be well settled.
notes: The home needs only an ordinary standard and must be tidy, clean and safe.

rule_summary: The home must have room for a foster child. In most cases this means the child should have their own bedroom, but there can be discretion.
notes: Oslo kommune asks emergency homes for a separate room for the child.

rule_summary: Oslo kommune asks emergency foster carers to have a driving licence and a car, and to live no more than an hour's drive from Oslo city centre.
notes: Applies to Oslo's emergency homes only.

rule_summary: Anyone to be approved as a foster parent must present a full, extended police certificate. Others who live in the home can be asked for a limited certificate.
notes: Read in the act as passed by the Storting (Lovvedtak 173 (2020–2021)). Lovdata, which holds the current consolidated text, does not allow automated reading (robots.txt). Later amendments were checked only in Lovvedtak 125 (2024–2025). The same applies to people who take children into respite homes.

rule_summary: Bufdir says the certificate is an extended child-care certificate, which also shows reports, penalty notices, fines and time-barred cases. Violence and abuse always rule a person out; other entries are judged case by case.
notes: Entries that raise doubt about suitability mean a person cannot be approved.

rule_summary: A health certificate and an extended police certificate are gathered for all adults in the family before the child moves in.
Applicants must present a full police certificate. Applicants who have lived abroad must also give a police certificate from that country.
notes: Read in the act as passed by the Storting (Lovvedtak 104 (2016–2017)). Lovdata, which holds the current consolidated text, does not allow automated reading (robots.txt). Bufdir's page asks for a certificate from each country where the applicants have lived.

rule_summary: After the self-presentation form arrives, the foster care service checks with the child welfare services where you have lived. It also gets information from NAV if you have had support or benefits.
Asker kommune gathers information from references, the local NAV office and the child welfare service as part of its own approval.
notes: A municipal page. We found no national rule on the number of references.

rule_summary: The steps are a first contact or information meeting, a written self-presentation, a talk and a home visit, then the Solid training with its assessment, and a final social work assessment that may recommend you as a foster home.
notes: Then matching with a child, health and police certificates, and formal approval by the municipality. Applicants must agree to the service seeing information from NAV, child welfare and, if relevant, doctors and police.

rule_summary: During the Solid training, applicants take part in three assessment meetings, two of them at home, with home tasks before each meeting.
notes: In Oslo the city's Barne- og familieetaten runs the training and assessment instead of Bufetat.

rule_summary: The child welfare service in the responsible municipality chooses a foster home that suits the child and approves it. If the home is in another municipality, the two can agree that the home's municipality approves it.
notes: Read in the act as passed by the Storting (Lovvedtak 173 (2020–2021)). Lovdata, which holds the current consolidated text, does not allow automated reading (robots.txt). Later amendments were checked only in Lovvedtak 125 (2024–2025).

rule_summary: Bufetat's assessment units talk with applicants, at home and at Bufetat's office, and write a social report (sosialrapport). They look at personal qualities and motivation, health, ability to care for the child through childhood, family situation, finances, housing and conduct.
legal_citation: Forskrift om adopsjon (FOR-2018-06-22-959) § 1; Bufdir Rundskriv 2020-08 (adoption casework), sections 5 and 8.6.3
notes: Bufdir's adoption circular, last revised June 2026, read on bufdir.no. Bufetat may also ask its advisory doctor or psychologist for an opinion.

rule_summary: Bufetat, not the municipality, carries out the home study. The municipality helps only if Bufetat asks, for example to shed light on an application, to get the child's consent or to write follow-up reports.
legal_citation: Adopsjonsloven (LOV-2017-06-16-48) §§ 9, 19 and 23; Bufdir Rundskriv 2020-08 (adoption casework), section 5.4
notes: Bufdir's adoption circular, last revised June 2026, read on bufdir.no.

rule_summary: Foster parents must complete training before the child moves in, in line with national professional recommendations. Bufetat gives this training to all foster homes recruited by municipalities and by Bufetat.
notes: Read in Bufdir's summary of the regulations; the section number was not checked. Lovdata, which holds the current consolidated text, does not allow automated reading (robots.txt).

rule_summary: The basic training is called Solid. It mixes e-learning, group sessions and assessment meetings, and usually takes three months. Both adults in the home must take part; children at home are offered parts of it.
notes: Topics include child welfare and foster care, child development and trauma, caring for a foster child, the effect on your family, and working with the child's parents. Taking part does not commit you to fostering.

rule_summary: Everyone who applies to adopt from abroad or to adopt a Norwegian-born infant must first take a preparatory course run by Bufetat. It is two weekends, 3 to 5 weeks apart, and couples attend together.
notes: People who have taken the course before, or adopted from abroad before, need not take it again. For adoption through an organisation, a confirmation from the organisation is needed to get a place.

rule_summary: Bufetat runs further courses for foster carers on contact with the child's family, children affected by adults' substance use, minority backgrounds, fostering teenagers, and trauma-informed care.
notes: Courses are held as needed. Many municipalities also offer group guidance or courses.

rule_summary: Most foster homes are ordinary municipal foster homes, including homes in the child's family or network. Emergency homes and specialised foster homes are full-time roles under an agreement with Bufetat or Oslo kommune.
notes: Visiting or respite homes (besøkshjem, avlastningshjem) are a support measure, not foster homes; people contact their municipality about them.

rule_summary: Since 2026 the child welfare and health tribunal can decide that a child will stay in the foster home for good (varig opphold i fosterhjem). The child must have lived there for at least 2 years and the foster parents must agree.
notes: Read in Lovvedtak 125 (2024–2025), the 'quality lift' amendments. Bufdir lists these changes as in force from 1 January 2026. A child over 12 must also agree, and the foster parents must have shown they can raise the child as their own.

rule_summary: Prior consent to adopt from abroad covers one child under 5, or two siblings who are both under 5.
notes: Read in the act as passed by the Storting (Lovvedtak 104 (2016–2017)). Lovdata, which holds the current consolidated text, does not allow automated reading (robots.txt). The consent names the organisation and the country of origin.

rule_summary: An emergency home has a full-time agreement with Bufetat for a 5-year period, on the same terms as state employees.
notes: Oslo kommune has its own terms for emergency homes.

rule_summary: A specialised foster home has a full-time agreement with Bufetat that lasts 3 years at a time.
notes: Oslo kommune's specialised foster homes have 5-year agreements.

rule_summary: The basic training and assessment take on average 3 months. After that, the time until a child moves in varies.
notes: Matching depends on which children need a home and on the family's own views.

rule_summary: Bufetat's assessment of applicants normally takes 3 to 4 months.
notes: The value is the upper end of the range. The same is stated for Norwegian-born infants.

rule_summary: Prior consent lasts 3 years. It can be extended once, by 2 years, if applied for at least 3 months before it ends.
notes: Bufdir says the whole process can take several years, and some must start again after five years.

rule_summary: Applicants to adopt a Norwegian-born infant who have been assessed stay on Bufdir's register for one year, and only once.
notes: People who have already adopted a Norwegian-born infant can register again so the child can have a sibling. Fewer than ten children born in Norway are adopted each year.

rule_summary: The child welfare service must consider whether someone in the child's family or close network can be the foster home, using network methods where suitable.
notes: Read in the act as passed by the Storting (Lovvedtak 173 (2020–2021)). Lovdata, which holds the current consolidated text, does not allow automated reading (robots.txt). Later amendments were checked only in Lovvedtak 125 (2024–2025). Bufdir's support page says Bufetat can give municipalities family group conference (familieråd) coordinators.

rule_summary: Relatives and friends are assessed against the same requirements, but the child welfare service can use more discretion and add support to make up for gaps. They get the same pay, rights and follow-up as other foster homes.
notes: They take the same Solid training, partly adapted. It is not unusual for the child to move in before training starts.

rule_summary: The allowance follows each child: carers of two foster children get two allowances, with no reduction.
notes: Existing carers who want another child are assessed again, including how the child already living there would be affected.

rule_summary: As a guide, a new adoptive child should be 2 years younger than the youngest child in the family. Applicants should usually wait until the last child to arrive has been in the family for at least 1 year.
notes: Bufdir's adoption circular (Rundskriv 2020-08, section 8.6.3) gives the same 2-year guide.

rule_summary: Foster carers get a monthly basic allowance (grunnstøtte) for taking on the role. It equals the National Insurance basic amount (G) a year, which from 1 July 2026 is NOK 11,379 a month.
notes: The basic allowance is taxable and earns National Insurance pension. KS publishes the detailed guide rates; ks.no does not allow automated reading (robots.txt). Stavanger kommune gives NOK 136,549 a year.

rule_summary: A tax-free expense allowance (utgiftsdekning) covers day-to-day costs such as food, clothes, housing, leisure and holidays. From 1 July 2026 the guide rate starts at NOK 7,288 a month for the youngest children.
notes: Rates rise with the child's age. KS publishes the detailed guide rates; ks.no does not allow automated reading (robots.txt).

rule_summary: From 1 July 2026 the guide expense allowance for children over 15 is NOK 10,733 a month.
notes: KS publishes the detailed guide rates; ks.no does not allow automated reading (robots.txt).

rule_summary: The child welfare service must pay foster parents an allowance and cover their expenses. It must also compensate for lost occupational pension when carers are fully or partly out of other work because of the role.
notes: Read in Lovvedtak 125 (2024–2025), the 'quality lift' amendments. Bufdir lists these changes as in force from 1 January 2026.

rule_summary: The level of payment is agreed with the child welfare service, and KS rates are a guide. Decisions on pay, release from work and respite are individual decisions that carers can appeal to the county governor (Statsforvalteren).
notes: The child welfare service must tell foster parents about the right to appeal.

rule_summary: Child benefit (barnetrygd) is paid to the foster parents on top of the expense allowance, and the child welfare service pays necessary extra costs. Foster parents do not get cash-for-care benefit (kontantstøtte).
Foster parents with daily care of a child under 6 get a yearly pension credit equal to 4.5 G in National Insurance.
notes: Foster parents do not get the mandatory occupational pension that employers pay.

rule_summary: Bufetat's emergency and specialised foster homes are paid at least 4.3 G a year for one adult, set by length of experience and assessed individually. Emergency homes are paid every month whether or not a child is placed.
notes: Both also get expenses, respite and holiday. The specialised foster home page gives the same minimum.

rule_summary: Oslo kommune pays emergency homes at least 4.5 G a year. Specialised foster homes start at 4.7 G for unqualified carers or 5.2 G for qualified carers.
notes: The emergency home figure is on Oslo's emergency home page. Both add tax-free expenses.

rule_summary: Parents who adopt a child from abroad get a one-off state adoption grant after the child arrives. In 2026 it is NOK 130,160.
notes: Bufdir sends the application form after the adoption is registered.

rule_summary: Adoptive parents have the right to leave, parental benefit, child benefit and cash-for-care benefit.
notes: Details are with NAV.

rule_summary: The Solid training is free. People with a long journey to the group sessions are offered a hotel stay.
The preparatory course is free: Bufetat pays for board and lodging, and participants pay their own travel.
Costs of adopting from abroad vary. Applicants pay fees in Norway and abroad, translation, and travel to collect the child, in instalments.
notes: Bufdir sends readers to Adopsjonsforum for its rates for Colombia.

rule_summary: People whose usual home is in Norway need prior consent from the adoption authority to adopt a child from abroad.
notes: Read in the act as passed by the Storting (Lovvedtak 104 (2016–2017)). Lovdata, which holds the current consolidated text, does not allow automated reading (robots.txt). Applications go by post to the Bufetat region where the applicants live.

rule_summary: Oslo kommune recruits foster homes in Oslo and nearby, up to 2 hours' travel from the city.
notes: Elsewhere, each Bufetat region recruits in its own counties.

rule_summary: For specialised and emergency foster homes, it is desirable that an adult has relevant education, work experience or earlier experience as a foster carer.
notes: These homes must first be approved as ordinary foster homes and complete the basic training.

rule_summary: Foster parents must have particular ability, time and energy to give children a safe and good home.
notes: Read in the act as passed by the Storting (Lovvedtak 173 (2020–2021)). Lovdata, which holds the current consolidated text, does not allow automated reading (robots.txt). Later amendments were checked only in Lovvedtak 125 (2024–2025).

rule_summary: Bodø kommune quotes the foster home regulations: foster parents must have a stable life, generally good health and good cooperation skills, and finances, housing and a social network that let the child thrive.
notes: Read as quoted on a municipal page; the section number was not checked. Lovdata, which holds the current consolidated text, does not allow automated reading (robots.txt).

rule_summary: You cannot have active child welfare measures for your own children when you start the process.
Foster parents work under a commission agreement and count as contractors, not employees. They earn no holiday pay, and get sick pay only after 17 days.
notes: Bufdir suggests settling extra insurance for the first 17 days in the foster home agreement.

rule_summary: The child welfare service cannot use a foster home that has an agreement with a private provider about pay or the content of the role. Bufetat can buy specialised and emergency foster homes from private providers.
notes: Read in Lovvedtak 125 (2024–2025), the 'quality lift' amendments. Bufdir lists these changes as in force from 1 January 2026. Bufdir's support page says the same and refers to Prop. 86 L (2021–2022). Municipalities can still buy respite and guidance services.

rule_summary: The child welfare service and the foster parents must sign a written foster home agreement. Bufdir's template must be used after a care order.
notes: Read in the act as passed by the Storting (Lovvedtak 173 (2020–2021)). Lovdata, which holds the current consolidated text, does not allow automated reading (robots.txt). Later amendments were checked only in Lovvedtak 125 (2024–2025). The template is on Bufdir's page on the foster home agreement.

rule_summary: The responsible municipality follows up the child and the foster family for as long as the child lives there. Bufdir says the child welfare service must visit at least four times a year.
notes: Bufetat follows up the emergency and specialised homes it provides. Support can include guidance, release from work and a visiting home.

rule_summary: The municipality where the foster home is must supervise each child from move-in until age 18. An independent supervisor (tilsynsperson) visits at least four times a year and reports to the child welfare service.
notes: The law's wording was checked in Lovvedtak 173 (2020–2021) and Lovvedtak 125 (2024–2025) on stortinget.no.

rule_summary: A young person can stay in the foster home as aftercare until 25 if they and the carers wish, and the agreement can continue.
notes: Bufdir says it will often be natural to keep the same level of pay after the child turns 18.

rule_summary: When the child welfare service has a care order, the child welfare and health tribunal decides on an adoption by the foster parents. Foster care payments stop when the adoption is final.
notes: Bufetat then issues the adoption order without testing the conditions again.
